newsitem.title: USA: U.S. balloonist over Egypt, not giving up quest.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist over Egypt, not giving up quest.

text.p: American adventurer Steve Fossett was over Egypt on Saturday, refusing to call off his quest to make man's first nonstop global balloon flight despite a detour which cost him heavily in both speed and fuel.

At 7:30 a.m. EST (1230 GMT) Fossett's control centre at Loyola University of Chicago said he had just crossed into Egypt from Sudan on a favourable wind that had him racing along at 143 miles per hour (230 kph).

Project manager Bo Kemper said the 52-year-old commodities broker had not formally abandoned his goal despite Friday's developments in which Libya at first denied him permission to fly over that country and relented three hours after Fossett had already detoured south.

Kemper said Fossett and his "Solo Spirit" balloon altered course after the Libyans changed signals and that he was over that country for an hour and 45 minutes as he headed back north to catch more powerful jet streams.
Asked where the expedition was going to wind up, Kemper said:
"We don't know. It keeps changing. Before we thought he'd ... likely have to put down in India. Now we wonder if we can squeeze more out of it."

He said the Libyan government notified the staff of British tycoon Richard Branson about its change of position. Branson, whose own attempt at the globe-circling record ended in failure earlier this month, had attempted to intercede earlier with the Libyans on Fossett's behalf.
"We are very appreciative of the Libyan government to grant permission, even at a late date," Kemper said. "We appreciate the generosity of the government"

On Friday, after Fossett was forced to detour, Kemper said India looked like the most logical end point for the journey, if weather conditions stalled Fossett's progress. If he winds up there he would have made it roughly half way around the world.
The dip south of Libya probably cost Fossett fuel that he planned on using to complete his crossing of the Pacific back to the United States, in addition to putting him in a slower wind pattern.
The U.S. State Department had condemned Libya's initial refusal to let Fossett cross the country, saying it reflected the "paranoia of the Libyan leadership."

Whatever the outcome, Kemper still had a chance at setting a record for duration. The current mark for time spent in a balloon is six days and 16 minutes set in 1981 by Richard Abruzzo and Troy Bradley. Fossett's trip began late on Monday night in St. Louis.
On Friday, Fossett broke his own record for balloon distance travel when he passed 5,435 miles (8,747 km) over Algeria. Kemper set the earlier mark on a voyage from South Korea to Canada.
